summary:
MindOrbit is a mental-wellbeing support tool that works on board the spacecraft, even when Earth cannot respond. On distant missions, communication can be delayed or cut off entirely at any moment. Astronauts face months of isolation and confinement, and NASA recognizes behavioral-health risk and the lack of autonomous support tools as open gaps.

MindOrbit analyzes the sentiment of the astronaut’s free-text diary and combines it with three sensor indicators: sleep, activity and resting heart rate. Each day is compared with the astronaut’s own wellbeing baseline, not a population average. The system produces a 0–100 risk index with the reasons behind it, gives immediate supportive feedback, suggests guided activities and shows which mental-health areas need attention. When a connection is available, it sends the psychosocial team on Earth a report and history that protect the astronaut’s privacy and confidentiality. The diary text never leaves the spacecraft.

This matters because, on a long mission, mental health is part of safety: it affects sleep, morale and decision-making. Detecting small changes early lets the crew and ground teams act preventively, before a crisis, and keeps support available even when Earth is out of reach. The prototype runs on simulated crew data.
details:
What it does and how it works
The astronaut writes a free-text diary in a single box. On board, with no internet needed, MindOrbit reads the text (themes and tone, with a negation rule) and cross-checks it with three sensor indicators: hours of sleep, minutes of activity and resting heart rate. Each day is measured against the astronaut’s own wellbeing baseline (the deviation from their personal pattern), and the system tracks how many days the same theme repeats within a 7-day window. A diary theme confirmed by a sensor weighs more. The result is a 0–100 risk index (35% tone, 35% persistence, 30% sensors) in green, yellow and red bands, always with the reason explained in plain language.

The response to the astronaut is immediate: a warm message that always suggests an action, and a guided activity, with a timer when it fits, chosen from the day’s theme. The astronaut can confirm or correct the detected mood and follow a 14-day history. If the index reaches red, the app guides them to the medical officer and triggers an immediate report.

The link with Earth. Weekly, or right away in case of red, the system builds a report with aggregated data only: no diary text, with a pseudonym, compressed, encrypted (Fernet) and integrity-checked (SHA-256). It goes into a queue that simulates the real Earth–Mars signal delay, calculated from NASA/JPL orbital data, and that holds packets during communication blackouts. On Earth, the psychosocial team sees a clinical panel with the history, the breakdown of the index and the contexts that keep repeating, and sends guidance back, with read receipts. Onboard support never depends on this exchange.

Main features.

  • Onboard support (astronaut tab): a single-box free diary with no minimum length; daily sensor reading (the astronaut never sees future days); a personal wellbeing baseline for each crew member; detection of seven themes (tiredness and sleep, anxiety, low mood, homesickness and isolation, crew conflict, overload, monotony); tone analysis from -1 to +1 with a negation rule; 7-day theme persistence, with an alert from 4 days; sensor cross-check; and the 0–100 risk index with its plain-language reason.
  • Immediate care: warm feedback after every entry, with no clinical labels and always with an action; a guided countermeasure for each theme (sleep routine, 3-minute guided breathing, a pleasant activity, a recorded message for family, time alone, a planned break, a new activity), with a next-day check on whether it helped; a mood of the day that the astronaut can confirm or correct; a 14-day personal history; and, in red, guidance to the crew medical officer.
  • Transparency for the astronaut: a notice of what is shared with Earth (categories only, never the diary text) and a box that receives and marks guidance from Earth as read.
  • Link and Earth panel: weekly and immediate reports; encryption with integrity checking (a changed byte makes the packet be rejected); a delay queue with the real Earth–Mars delay and communication blackouts; a clinical panel with the full history, the index breakdown and recurring contexts; guidance sent back to the astronaut; and read receipts.
  • Demo controls and quality: advance the simulated mission day, turn a blackout on and off, set the delay (real or manual) and restart the demo (each visitor gets a private temporary database starting at day 1); a bilingual interface (English and Portuguese); offline operation, no GPU needed, and under 1 second to analyze an entry; and automated tests for the analysis core, privacy, the link and the interface. The diary analysis currently works in Portuguese.

Benefits and intended impact. Detecting strain early, while preventive action is still possible; keeping support available when Earth cannot respond; giving astronauts autonomy and privacy over what they write; and giving the ground team an objective history to define preventive action protocols and direct communication. In the long run, the goal is a support tool for space exploration missions.

Tools. Python 3.11, Streamlit (interface), pandas and numpy (data and calculations), Altair (charts), SQLite (local storage), the cryptography library (encryption) and pytest (automated tests). It is software only: it runs on an ordinary laptop with no specific hardware, and no dependency reaches the internet during use.

Creative aspect. Instead of comparing the astronaut with an average, MindOrbit compares the person with themselves, and joins what they write with what their body shows. We also designed the separation between the ship and Earth as a real privacy border: the diary text never leaves the spacecraft, and only what the psychosocial team needs to care and intervene crosses the link. In addition, mental health follows the real needs of human beings, which gives it social and economic relevance when we think about space projects.

What we considered. Autonomy (support works without Earth), privacy (aggregates and a pseudonym only, none of the text), a warm tone always paired with an action, and transparency (every alert shows its reason). The rules (word lists, weights and bands) live in configuration files so they can be calibrated. The prototype uses simulated data from a four-person crew over 180 days, and the next steps are real sensors, space analog data such as HERA, and a local language model in place of the word lists.
